transcript.text:
Try these quick checks:

1. Check power
• Make sure it’s plugged in under the sink.
• Check the kitchen breaker/GFCI outlet. Reset any tripped breaker or GFCI button.
• If it’s hardwired, don’t open electrical panels—check the breaker only.

2. Make sure the door is fully latched
• Push the door firmly closed.
• Check for dishes/racks blocking it.
• A failed or misaligned door latch can make the dishwasher appear completely dead.

3. Turn off Control Lock / Child Lock
• Look for a lock icon. Usually hold the button marked Lock, Heated Dry, or Start for about 3 seconds, depending on model.

4. Reset it
• Turn off the dishwasher breaker for 5 minutes, then turn it back on.
• Alternatively, some models reset by holding Start/Cancel for 3–5 seconds.

5. Check the control panel
• If lights come on but it won’t start, select a cycle and press Start, then close the door promptly—many models require this.
• If there are no lights at all after confirming power, the issue may be the outlet, wiring, door switch, thermal fuse, or control board.

If you tell me the brand/model and whether it has any lights or display, I can narrow it down.
It's a Neff integrated one, 6 years old. No lights or display at all, totally dead. Other sockets and lights in the kitchen work and nothing's tripped on the consumer unit. Door is shut firmly too.

For a Neff integrated dishwasher that is completely dead (no LEDs/display), the most likely causes are loss of supply at the appliance, a blown fuse in its connection spur/plug, or a failed control-module power supply.

Safe checks you can do:

1. Find its local power connection
   Integrated dishwashers are often plugged into a socket in the cupboard next to it, or supplied through a switched fused spur (a small wall switch with a fuse drawer), rather than the visible kitchen sockets.

2. Check the fused spur/plug
• If there is a fused spur, switch it off first at the consumer unit, then check/replace its fuse with the same rating (commonly 13 A, but use what is fitted/specified).
• If it has a normal plug, again isolate power first, then inspect the plug fuse and lead for damage.
• Don’t fit a larger fuse “to see if it works.”

3. Test the dishwasher socket — only if safely accessible
   With the dishwasher unplugged, a known-working lamp/charger can confirm whether that specific socket has power. The kitchen sockets working does not necessarily mean the dishwasher’s dedicated outlet/spur is live.

4. Try a full isolation reset
   Turn the dishwasher circuit off at the consumer unit for 10 minutes, then restore it. This occasionally clears a failed control-board state, though a completely blank panel usually points to a power issue rather than a normal programme fault.

If power is definitely reaching the dishwasher and it remains totally blank, it will likely need an appliance engineer. On a six-year-old Neff (BSH group), common culprits include the main control board/internal low-voltage power supply, wiring connection, or less commonly the door-switch wiring. A door latch fault can stop a cycle starting, but usually would not by itself make the display entirely dead.

Avoid pulling the integrated unit out unless you are comfortable doing so—water hoses, drain hose and cabinet fixings need to be dealt with properly.
There's a switch above the worktop and it's on, with the little neon light lit. I don't know how to check the fuse in it though, and I've no spare or meter. I can't pull the dishwasher out either.

That sounds like a switched fused spur supplying the dishwasher. The neon being lit shows the spur has an incoming supply, but it does not always prove the fuse is intact or that power is reaching the dishwasher.

You can check the fuse without pulling the dishwasher out:

1. Turn off the dishwasher/kitchen circuit at the consumer unit — or the main switch if you cannot identify the correct circuit.
2. Confirm the little neon on the worktop switch is now off.
3. Look closely at the front/bottom edge of the spur switch. There is usually a small fuse drawer/carrier, often marked “FUSE,” with a notch.
4. Use a small flat screwdriver or a fingernail in the notch to gently pull the carrier out. Do not remove the switch faceplate or touch wiring.
5. The fuse is normally a small ceramic cartridge, usually 13 A for a dishwasher (check the marking on the old fuse/carrier).

Without a meter or a spare fuse, you may not be able to confirm it has failed: ceramic fuses often do not visibly show damage. Don’t substitute a higher-rated fuse or try to bypass it.

If you have a neighbour/family member with a known good 13 A BS 1362 fuse, you could replace it like-for-like after checking the old one’s rating. If the replacement blows or the dishwasher remains dead, stop there and call an electrician or appliance engineer.

If you’d rather not touch the spur at all, the practical next step is an electrician first: they can quickly confirm whether 230 V is leaving the spur and arriving at the dishwasher. If it is, then it is likely an internal dishwasher fault—commonly the Neff/BSH control module power supply—rather than the kitchen electrics.
